opening.headline: Design a single flow of evaluation criteria that changes must pass before they go live, as well as incremental deployment and rollback paths that limit the impact once they go live.
body: Say you fix one line of the prompt and your quality plummets for some customers. Fixes were confirmed with just a few check-in conversations in the development environment and deployed to all customers at once. It was difficult to know which customer groups had worsened and how much worse it had become, and there was no way to immediately return to the previous state.

In this lesson, we'll start by looking at what an evaluation gate is and what evaluations are used for it. We then look at promoting and reverting prompts to environment-specific versions and nameplates, managing deployments declaratively with Databricks bundles, and canaries and shadow deployments. At the end, we explain examples of reading sudden drops hidden in the average and why gradual distribution is necessary even after passing the evaluation.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain what risks evaluation gates and incremental deployments each prevent
You can design your release flow by linking promotion and rollback paths with evaluation criteria.

screens.title: Quality plummeted for some customers after changing prompts
screens.lead: Switch the toggle to compare how quality has changed for each customer group before and after deployment.

visual.alt: Before deployment, all customer groups were at similar heights, and after deployment, only the customer group inquiring about refunds was significantly lowered.
labels: There is no significant difference in the average

states.label: Before distribution
states.body: Before uploading the fix, I confirmed it through several inspection conversations in the development environment. For common questions like general inquiries and order inquiries, the response seemed better than before. It is not apparent at this point that the conversation used for confirmation was small and biased. The passing criteria were not set in advance, so judgment was left to intuition.

states.label: After deployment
states.body: The change applied to all customers at once. A few days later, only those customers who inquired about refunds complained that quality had plummeted. The overall average didn't drop much, so it wasn't noticeable at first, and it took time to see how much worse off some customer groups were. There was no immediate path back to the previous state, so the damage was prolonged. This lesson covers two layers of mechanisms that prevent this thinking: evaluation gates before raising and progressive distribution after raising.

screens.title: Think About It: Could It Be Turned Back?
screens.lead: Look at each question, think of your own answer first, and then select an item to see what you can think about. You will not enter or submit an answer.

items.prompt: Have you seen similar situations where quality plummeted for some customers after changing the prompt?
items.answer: Quality problems often appear first with some, but not all, types of input. If you've ever seen something like that, think back and see what input types were missing at the time to see how you need to broaden your evaluation case.

items.prompt: Was there a passing criteria before posting the change, or was it just a gut feeling?
items.answer: If the standard is not set in advance, whether to post it or not will depend on the mood of the day. The evaluation gate is a promise to set the passing criteria as a predetermined indicator rather than human intuition.

items.prompt: When the problem surfaced, how long did it take to get things back to where they were before?
items.answer: The longer the reversal time, the longer the damage. If you let operations read the label rather than pointing directly to the version number, you can revert to a previous state simply by moving the label. Confirm this structure in the following screen.

screens.title: Evaluation Gate: Must pass to be promoted
screens.lead: Move on to the next step and see what the evaluation gate produces and in what order.

visual.alt: A cyclical structure from evaluation cases to inference, trace, metrics, analysis, and optimization.

steps.title: Evaluation case definition
steps.body: An evaluation case is a specification of what the agent must do and the expected results. It can have one or multiple conversation steps, and can also contain the context of the conversation and ways to mimic user responses. Using scenario creation and user simulation, you can create multi-turn inspection dialogs even without existing test data.

steps.title: Inference execution and trace
steps.body: The actual execution of the evaluation case is reasoning. For each execution, the agent's behavior is left as a trace. A trace is a factual record of model inputs, responses, and tool calls, providing a basis for later tracking back at what stage you made a mistake.

steps.title: Indicator calculation
steps.body: For each trace, metrics are calculated using pre-built evaluators or custom evaluators. There are metrics that require an example of a correct answer (such as Exact Match) and metrics that just look at the trace without a correct answer (such as Was this helpful). The latter can also be applied to traces collected from operations.

steps.title: Analysis and Optimization
steps.body: Find key problems by reading indicators and judgments, and connect those problems with evaluation cases to get directions for improvement. Optimization, which runs this process automatically, analyzes the results, suggests agent improvement plans, and re-evaluates and confirms them. The point of the gate is that the criteria for passing all these judgments are not human senses, but predetermined indicators.

steps.title: At what point do you put it in?
steps.body: The evaluation can be done at two points in time. During development, you can evaluate agents locally to quickly fix prompts and tools, and once deployed, measure quality by analyzing historical traces or running synthetic benchmarks. The document divides assessments into three types depending on their purpose. These include rapid evaluation to quickly check agent logic or model changes, test case evaluation to check regression with a set data set (regular execution in CI/CD), and online monitoring to continuously monitor agents in operation. The gate just before promotion serves to prevent changes that do not meet the standards from advancing.

screens.outro: Next, we will compare how the gate makes decisions and what defects are caught by each evaluation method.

screens.title: Evaluators and automatic evaluation
screens.lead: Select each tab to see how each evaluation method catches different types of defects.

tabs.label: Reference-based and reference-free indicators
tabs.body: Indicators are broadly divided into two categories. Reference-based indicators require assessment cases with examples of correct answers, and then compare the responses to those correct answers. An example is Exact Match, which looks for an exact match. Indicators without references are judged by looking at only the trace without the correct answer, and an example is an indicator that asks whether it was helpful, such as Helpfulness. The latter can also be applied to traces collected from operational traffic. In both methods, problems that arise when conversations are long require separate multi-turn evaluation.

tabs.label: Multi-turn evaluation
tabs.body: The judgment is made by looking at the entire conversation history. The automatic evaluator extracts the user's intent and dynamically creates a rubric to suit the situation to make an objective decision. Catch defects over several turns, such as whether instructions were followed, tools were used properly, and tasks were successful.

tabs.label: environmental simulation
tabs.body: It intercepts certain tool calls made by the agent and intentionally injects conditions such as HTTP 503 errors or increased latency. You can check how your agents respond when external tools fail or slow down, without impacting operations.

tabs.label: Failure cluster analysis
tabs.body: Cases that fail the assessment are grouped into failure clusters to reveal key problem types. Even if failures seem scattered, grouping them into clusters allows you to check whether they come from the same cause, and connects which evaluation case points to that problem, which can be used to prioritize improvement.

screens.title: Deployment, promotion, and rollback of prompts by environment
screens.lead: Move the slider to see how your name tag moves between environments and its rollback path. This screen does not describe the functionality of a specific product, but rather is an example assuming a general design that labels the prompt version.

visual.alt: Illustration of prompt versions 1 through 5 and dev, staging, and prod labels indicating different versions.

stops.body: Prompts, like code, have versions. Each modification will result in a new version and the old version will remain. This will allow you to compare what has changed and go back to a previous version if necessary.

The new version is first indicated by an alias in the development environment. The production service reads the environment nameplate rather than the version number, so which version you use in development has no effect on operations.

stops.value: After passing the gate, go to staging
stops.body: Only versions that pass the evaluation gate can be moved to the next environment's nameplate. If the standards are not met, the name plate will remain on the previous version and the new version will not be promoted. Promotion is not about modifying the code, but about moving the name tag.

Move versions that have been further verified in staging to the production nameplate. In this case, it is also safer to use it with gradual deployment rather than changing the whole thing at once. There should be a record of who moved to which version and when.

If problems are revealed in operation, revert the nameplate to a previous version. The rollback time is short because you don't have to redeploy your code. Since previous versions must not be erased, the version to be rolled back must be retained for a certain period of time and the ability to move nameplates must be restricted.

screens.outro: Rather than being limited to prompts, deployment of entire code and settings can be managed in a declarative manner called bundles.

screens.title: Databricks bundle: validate, deploy, run
screens.lead: Read the commands for dealing with Databricks bundles (documented as Declarative Automation Bundles) from top to bottom to see the order in which the bundle life cycle occurs.

data.code:
#1. Verify that the bundle configuration file is correct
databricks bundle validate

#2. Deploy to development target
databricks bundle deploy -t dev

#3. Run the deployed workflow (resource key is an example)
databricks bundle run -t dev my_job

#4. Once confirmed, upload in the order of staging and operation.
databricks bundle deploy -t staging
databricks bundle deploy -t prod

#5. Permanently delete bundles that are no longer used.
databricks bundle destroy -t dev

notes.note: validate verifies that the bundle configuration file is syntactically correct and has valid definitions, and by default shows a summary of identifying information such as bundle name, target, and workspace. This is a check done first before deploying or running.
deploy uploads a bundle to the workspace of the specified target. This is usually tested first in the developer's development workspace.
run executes a workflow (e.g. job) defined in the deployed bundle. Deployment and execution are separated, so you can check the execution results after uploading.

Once development is completed, the same bundle is promoted to staging and operation. The bundle tracks the state of created resources by ID rather than name, and removes resources missing from the configuration from the target.

destroy permanently deletes previously deployed jobs, pipelines, and artifacts and cannot be undone. There is a verification process by default, and deletion of certain resources can be prevented by setting lifecycle.

screens.outro: Bundles are a way to declare settings in YAML and upload them to source management, review, and CI/CD like code.

screens.title: Canary Deployment and Shadow Deployment
screens.lead: Switch the toggle to see how the same request breaks down between the two methods and compare the responses your users receive. Each state first explains product-unrelated principles, followed by an example of the behavior of Amazon SageMaker AI.

visual.alt: In Canary, the request is divided into two fleets, and in Shadow, the request is copied and the response of the new variant is discarded.

states.label: canary
states.body: Principle: Canary is an incremental deployment that exposes changes to only a portion of traffic over a set period of time and compares metrics with the rest (control group) to decide whether to keep going or stop. The smaller the exposure range, the less damaging a false change will be, and if the observed baking interval is too short or the sample is too small, the signal will be distorted. As a judgment indicator, select a small number of things that are close to user influence, such as error rate and delay, and set interruption conditions in advance. In LLM, the output varies for the same input, so the metrics fluctuate from request to request. So you should compare canaries and controls side by side at the same time and observe them until you have enough samples. If the prompt, model version, and settings are changed together, it is difficult to determine the cause by only reverting some of them, so all changes made together are grouped into one rollback unit. The explanation is based on canary traffic movement in Amazon SageMaker AI. In Canary, only a portion of traffic is sent to the new version (green fleet) and the rest is handled by the old version (blue fleet). Canaries can be of any size and must be no more than 50% of the new fleet capacity. During the baking period, if any pre-created CloudWatch alarms are monitored and any alarms sound, all traffic returns to the previous fleet. If not, the remaining traffic is moved to the new fleet. If a problem arises, it only affects the canary users.

states.label: shadow
states.body: Principle: Shadowing sends a copy of the actual request to a new version and returns only the response from the old version to the user. You can view delays and error rates from the actual input distribution without user influence. The caveat is that even if the response is discarded, the new version's behavior will actually occur. When a new version calls a tool to write data or send a message, there are side effects, so the write operation must be prevented or mocked, and each copy incurs an additional cost of calling the model. Shadow testing in SageMaker AI sends a copy of the request to a new variant within the same endpoint in real time, returning only the response from the production variant to the caller. Responses for new variants are either discarded or logged and compared offline. The advantage is that you can view operational metrics like latency and error rates without impacting your users. However, it cannot be applied to endpoints that use some functions such as serverless inference, asynchronous inference, and multi-model endpoints.

screens.title: Evaluation gate and incremental deployment in one release flow
screens.lead: Open the steps one by one to see what risks and stopping conditions each step prevents.

items.title: Step 1: Offline Evaluation Gate
items.body: Evaluate changes using prepared evaluation cases. If you don't meet the criteria, your upgrade will stop here, and this is the cheapest point with no impact to you. However, at this stage, only prepared cases are considered.

items.title: Step 2: Shadow
items.body: Send a copy of the actual operational request to the new version to check for delays and error rates. There will be no impact to users as they will only get the previous version of the response. Here we see differences in actual input distribution and load that offline evaluation does not see.

items.title: Stage 3: Canary
items.body: Expose new versions to only a subset of users and view alarms and quality metrics. If an alarm sounds, stop and revert to the previous version. The value of this step is that the impact is limited to a subset of users. The size and observation time of the canaries should be sufficient to be representative, and only one canary should be run at a time to determine which change is responsible.

items.title: Step 4: Full conversion and rollback path
items.body: Even after a full conversion, the previous version is retained for a period of time and the rollback path is kept open by nameplate. The conditions for passing each step should be pre-documented indicators, and exceptions to skipping a step should only be allowed within pre-agreed rules.

screens.title: Commentary 1: Read why quality has plummeted for only some customers
screens.lead: Open the case's diagnostic steps one by one to see how they reveal the plunge hidden in the average.

steps.title: situation
steps.body: The new prompts were more responsive for general customer questions, but quality plummeted for customers inquiring about refunds. This happened even though I passed the evaluation gate. It's not that the gate is broken, but it's what the gate saw that needs to be considered.

steps.title: Was there a refund in the evaluation case?
steps.body: First, check if there was a refund scenario in the evaluation case. Without it, the gate would not have been able to see the danger. Since the gate evaluates only what is contained in the case, the diversity of the cases is the gate's field of view.

steps.title: Scenario reinforcement
steps.body: Add vulnerable situations like refunds by creating scenarios. When creating a multi-turn conversation based on the agent's instructions, you can give the creation instructions specifically, such as a user requesting a refund. The reinforced case becomes a regression line of defense that is reused for all future changes.

steps.title: Break it down by customer group
steps.body: Instead of looking at the results as an average, try dividing them by customer group. Averages hide the sharp declines of minorities overshadowed by the good results of the majority. If you divide it into indicators for each customer group and check the cluster of failures, you can immediately see where things have gone bad.

steps.title: conclusion
steps.body: The quality of the gate depends on how diverse the evaluation cases are. The fact that you passed the evaluation only means that you did well in the scope of your preparation, and is not a guarantee that you did well in all inputs. So, as you can see in the following commentary, gradual distribution is also necessary.

screens.title: Explanation 2: Reasons for gradual deployment even after passing evaluation
screens.lead: Read what risks each strategy in the table prevents and to what extent, and see how the lines of defense overlap.

data.caption: Risks blocked and affected by each line of defense
rows: It doesn't see unprepared input and actual load
Delay and error rate in actual request copy
The new variant's responses do not go to the user, so there is no direct quality of experience, and it is not compatible with some endpoint features.
Alarms and quality from some real users
If you don't set alarm conditions in advance, you won't notice the problem.
Is it possible to revert to a previous version?
Total while reverting in case of problem
data.notes: Offline evaluation only looks at prepared cases, and the input distribution and load of actual operations may be different. Evaluation Gate is a proactive defense, Progressive Deployment is a reactive defense, and the two do not replace each other. If you set Canary's alarm conditions in advance, rollbacks occur automatically without waiting for human judgment. The indicators used in Canary are set to a small number of values ​​close to user influence, such as error rate and delay, and must be compared at the same time as the control group to avoid mixing in time zone effects.

screens.title: Commentary 3: Check release design to prevent promotion when evaluation fails
screens.lead: Select each check item and see what happens when that item is missing.

items.prompt: Is passing the evaluation automatically connected as a prerequisite for moving the name tag?
items.answer: If there is no connection, the name tag can be moved regardless of the evaluation results. On rush days, the gate is skipped, and you end up going back to the original situation where you raised it by guess. Passing or not must be a condition for promotion for the gate to have power.

items.prompt: Are bundle validation and deployment divided into development, staging, and operation?
items.answer: If it is not divided, settings that are not confirmed in development will go straight to production. By dividing the target and starting with development, configuration errors can be caught at an early stage, and distribution rights for operational targets can also be restricted separately.

items.prompt: Canary alarms include quality indicators and lead to automatic rollbacks
items.answer: If alarms only look at delay and error rate, they may respond quickly but miss changes that result in incorrect answers. Quality indicators should be included in the alarm, and when the alarm goes off, it should revert automatically rather than waiting for human approval to shorten the impact.

items.prompt: Is the version subject to rollback retained for a certain period of time?
items.answer: Once the previous version is cleaned up, there is no place to put the name tag back. Even after a complete conversion, the previous version must be maintained for a certain period of time, and the timing of cleanup must also be determined by rule.

screens.title: Key takeaways
screens.lead: Summarizes the content covered in this class in one place.

paragraphs: Evaluation gates are preliminary quality criteria that a change must pass before advancing to the next level. This involves defining evaluation cases, running inference to obtain traces, calculating metrics, and analyzing them to optimize them. The quality of the gate is determined by the variety of evaluation cases.

Evaluators and automated evaluations judge outputs and traces. Reference-based metrics compare to examples of correct answers, reference-free metrics look only at the trace, multi-turn evaluations look at the entire conversation, environmental simulations check resilience in situations like tool failures, and failure clusters reveal key problem types.

Promotes the prompt to a version- and environment-specific nameplate, and rolls back the nameplate back to the previous version. Bundles declare settings in YAML and manage deployment through validate, deploy, and run, in the order of development, staging, and operation.

Canaries and shadow deployments are reactive lines of defense that limit the impact even after passing the assessment. Evaluation gates and incremental distribution do not replace each other, and the passing conditions for each stage must be predetermined indicators.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: Before uploading, it is blocked with an evaluation gate, and after uploading, the impact is reduced through gradual distribution and rollback paths.

screens.title: Reflecting on Concept Cards
screens.lead: Select a card, turn it over, and summarize the key concepts one more time.

cards.back: This is a preliminary quality check that a change must pass before being promoted to the next level. The passing criteria are not human intuition, but predetermined indicators, and the more diverse the evaluation cases, the wider the gate's field of view.
It is a specification that describes the tasks the agent must perform and the expected results. It can contain one or multiple conversation steps, context, and ways to mimic user responses.

By having operations read the environment nameplate rather than the version number, moving the nameplate is a promotion and reverting to a previous version is a rollback. Records and permissions must go hand in hand.

A deployment that sends only a portion of traffic to the new version to ensure its safety. If the alarm does not sound during the baking period, the rest will move on, and if it does, it will return to the previous fleet.

It sends a copy of the request to the new variant and returns only the response from the production variant to the caller. View latency and error rates without user impact, but is not compatible with some endpoint features.

glossary.def: This is a preliminary quality check that a change must pass before it can be promoted.
This is an evaluation specification that describes the agent's tasks and expected results.
A deployment that sends only a portion of traffic to the new version to ensure its safety.
It sends a copy of the request to the new variant and returns only an operational response to the user.
This method declares the project's resources and settings in YAML and manages them with CLI.

misconceptions.myth: If you pass the evaluation, you can immediately distribute it in full.
misconceptions.fact: Since there are inputs that the evaluation case has not seen, incremental deployment is also needed.

misconceptions.myth: A good overall average is good for all customers.
misconceptions.fact: Breaking it down by customer group can reveal sharp drops hidden in the average.
The new variant's response will not be passed back to the user, so it will not affect the user directly.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: The assessment gate is a proactive defense and diversity of cases is important.
Prompts are promoted to environment-specific nameplates and rolled back.
Bundles manage deployments declaratively by validating, deploying, and running.
Canaries and Shadows are reactive lines of defense that limit the impact even after passing evaluation.

checks.q: The prod alias points to prompt version 4, and the new version 5 is not up to par. What is the appropriate action?
options: Move to 5 and revert if a problem arises.
Change the version number of the service code to 5.
Put the prod alias on 4 and don't promote 5 until it passes the criteria.
Skip the evaluation and apply to all customers at once
checks.explain: The evaluation gate is a preliminary defense that allows only the passed version to be moved to the next environment alias.

wrong.0: Exposing an inferior version first and then reverting it later goes against the purpose of the gate.
wrong.1: Promotion and rollback are easy when operations read aliases, not numbers.
wrong.3: If applied entirely without evaluation, problems such as a sharp drop in quality for some customers cannot be filtered out in advance.
